in_context.text: Paul has just warned that some will leave the faith for false teaching that forbids marriage and certain foods (4:1-3). He tells Timothy to remind the believers of this (4:6). Then, in this verse, he tells Timothy to turn away from worthless myths and to train himself in godliness instead.

speaker.text: Paul the apostle, who names himself as the writer. Many critical scholars think a follower wrote in Paul's name, while others defend Paul's authorship.

audience.text: Timothy, Paul's younger co-worker, whom Paul left to lead the church at Ephesus.

affected.text: The believers Timothy leads ("the brethren"), and by contrast the false teachers who spread lies and harsh rules.

what.text: Two commands: refuse godless, silly myths, and train yourself for godliness. Paul then explains that bodily training helps a little, but godliness helps in everything, for this life and the next.

events.text: While Timothy was leading the church at Ephesus, after Paul had gone on to Macedonia.

written.text: Traditional view: about AD 62-64, between Paul's two Roman imprisonments. Scholarly view: many critical scholars date it around AD 80-110.

where.text: Sent to Ephesus, a wealthy port city and capital of the Roman province of Asia, known for its temple of Artemis. The place of writing is not stated; possibly Macedonia.

purpose.text: Paul is equipping Timothy to resist false teaching. Instead of arguing over empty stories, Timothy should put his effort into a godly life and sound teaching.

big_picture.text: The letter holds that sound teaching produces godly living. Paul gives the same warning elsewhere: do not heed fables and endless genealogies (1 Timothy 1:4), and shun profane and vain babblings (2 Timothy 2:16).

for_readers.text: Godliness takes deliberate training, like an athlete's practice. It also means not letting fruitless speculation crowd out real faith and conduct.

why_it_matters.text: The word means myth or fiction, the opposite of a true account. Paul is rejecting invented stories that were being taught as religious truth, not stories in general.
This word means "old-womanish" and is glossed here as "silly." It marks the myths as trivial tales, not serious teaching.
It means unholy, the opposite of sacred. The myths are not merely foolish. They have nothing to do with God.
The word means to exercise or train the body or mind. Paul pictures godliness as something practiced with effort, which leads into his comparison with bodily training in 4:8.
It means piety or reverence toward God. It is a key word in this letter for the life that sound teaching produces.

takeaway.text: Don't waste your energy on empty religious myths. Put that effort into training yourself, day by day, in a life that honors God.

resolved.reason: The cited lexicon entry gives the meaning (exercise or train, originally to exercise naked) but says nothing about the word being the root of English "gymnasium."
resolved.fix: claim rewritten to match its sources
